overview.Module Title: Foundations of Computer Science and Engineering

sections.Aims and Fit of Module: This module allows students to become familiar with the foundational principles of computing and engineering. Students will get insight into the problem-solving mindset adopted by computer scientists and engineers to solve practical problems. It also serves to develop the English language, communication and study skills of students within the context of the relevant subject areas.
sections.Learning outcomes: A. Identify and explain the key concepts, principles, and theories in computer programming and engineering. B. Analyze and solve basic computing and engineering problems using fundamental problem-solving techniques. C. Demonstrate skills and techniques for effective study, including research, time management, and self-assessment, to support ongoing learning in computer science and engineering.
sections.Method of teaching and learning: Students will be expected to attend a weekly1-hour lecture and four 2-hour labs/tutorial sessions over the 6-week module duration. In the lectures, students will be introduced to academic and theoretical content as well as practical skills, which constitutes the subject of the module. In the tutorial/lab sessions, students are expected put into practice content and skills discussed in the lectures. This module will also help lay the English foundations that are necessary to work in an international environment in a technical field such as computing or engineering. In addition, students will be expected to devote approximately 61 hours of unsupervised time to work in the computer or engineering labs and to do private study. Time in labs will be devoted to work on learning activities and tasks related to the module, while private study will give time for students to reflect on the content of the lectures and conduct further background reading. There will be one final examination for the module which will be used to assess to what extent the theoretical content and practical skills have been learned.

offerings.heading: Engineering in Society: Systems, Sustainability, and Professional Context

listing.full_name: Engineering in Society: Systems, Sustainability, and Professional Context

overview.Module Title: Engineering in Society: Systems, Sustainability, and Professional Context

sections.Aims and Fit of Module: This module introduces students to the problem-solving mindset and system-level thinking adopted by engineers in professional contexts. Students develop the ability to analyse real-world engineering problems considering sustainability, ethical, economic, and societal factors. The module prepares students for further study and professional life by integrating engineering principles with collaborative project-based learning and effective communication.
sections.Learning outcomes: A Identify and explain the key principles of engineering systems, including sustainability, user-centred design, and professional context. B Analyse a real-world engineering problem and outline a solution using systems thinking and fundamental engineering techniques. C Plan and manage an engineering research project, communicating outcomes clearly and effectively in English through appropriate media.
sections.Method of teaching and learning: The module is delivered through a combination of weekly 1-hour lectures and fortnightly 2-hour laboratory sessions. Lectures introduce core technical content in engineering (e.g., sustainable systems, user‑centred design, intelligent engineering) alongside the professional and transferable skills required for the module’s project work. These include problem‑solving frameworks, systems thinking, project planning and management, and effective technical communication. Laboratory sessions provide supervised, hands-on opportunities for students to apply lecture content to practical engineering problems. Working in small teams, students engage in structured activities such as problem scoping, systems mapping, trade-off analysis, and preparation of project deliverables. Labs also serve as dedicated time for teams to advance their group project with instructor guidance. The module operates within a Research‑Led, Project‑Based Learning (RLPBL) framework. Students undertake a continuous group research pipeline that begins with a real‑world engineering problem, requires investigation of technical and contextual literature, and culminates in a collaborative technical artefact such as a poster or video. The RLPBL process is supported by guided independent study, where students conduct background reading, gather evidence from technical reports and sustainability frameworks, and refine their project outputs. An individual Project Readiness Checkpoint, scheduled early in the semester, assesses students’ grasp of foundational engineering concepts, problem-solving approaches, and project planning principles. Formative feedback from this checkpoint directly informs the final Group Project, where teams analyse a real-world engineering problem, propose reasoned solutions, and demonstrate clear communication of outcomes.
